findings.location: Results, paragraph 1
findings.quote: Premature discontinuations were reported in 9 patients due to loss to follow-up (9.6%).
findings.notes: grim_percentage returned `impossible`: 9 of 93 is 9.677%, which rounds to 9.7%, not 9.6%. A corroborating grim_sweep over every denominator up to the paper's own stated enrolment of 93 found 9.6% attainable only at n=52 (k=5), n=73 (k=7) and n=83 (k=8) -- so no denominator consistent with this trial reconciles a count of 9 with 9.6%. Both the numerator (9) and the denominator (93) are stated verbatim in the same paragraph, so no bound was assumed. grim_percentage is MCP-only and has no CLI verb, hence the reproduction command is the equivalent sweep. This GRIM-family `impossible` awaits the stage-2 R (`scrutiny`) cross-check. The consequence is nil: this is a one-digit rounding slip in a descriptive dropout figure and no claim depends on it.

consequence.explanation: A descriptive dropout percentage only; no inferential claim in the paper rests on it.

findings.location: Results, composite outcome paragraph (primary endpoint)

computed.bracketing_from_paper_own_SI: SI Annex 1 prints chi2=5.7111 -> p=0.05752 and chi2=6.082 -> p=0.04779, both at df=2
computed.day101_check: consistent -- chi2=5.732 sits just above SI's 5.7111 (p=0.05752), so p just under 0.0575 rounds to 0.06 as printed

findings.notes: This is a READING of printed values, not a recomputation -- no tool in this kit converts a chi-squared plus df to a p-value, and I did not compute one myself. The argument needs no arithmetic: with 3 groups, df=2 for both timepoints, and p is strictly decreasing in chi-squared. The paper's own Supplementary Annex 1 prints 44 chi-squared/p pairs from the same software at df=2, two of which bracket 5.833 -- chi2=5.7111 gives p=0.05752 and chi2=6.082 gives p=0.04779. A chi-squared of 5.833 must therefore yield p between 0.048 and 0.058, most likely ~0.054. The printed 0.54 is a factor-of-ten discrepancy consistent with a lost decimal point. Verified identical in BOTH the XML and the PDF (page 5), so it is not an extraction artifact. Note the companion Day 101 value is internally consistent, which isolates the error to the Day 180 figure.

consequence.explanation: The paper's conclusion of 'no significant differences' at Day 180 survives at the corrected p of ~0.054, but the printed 0.54 misstates the strength of evidence on a co-primary endpoint by an order of magnitude, making a borderline result look decisively null.

computed.surviving_bonferroni_within_outcome: Digit Span Backward at Day 180, group 1 (CRB+rTMS) vs group 3 (PLC+SHM), significant in BOTH ITT (0.0227) and PP (0.0423)

inputs.si_location: Supplementary Annex 1, DS_B_v2-baseline and TMT1_v2-baseline rows

findings.notes: The main text states twice that no subscale reached significance ('Individual outcomes scales are similar to composite findings'). The supplementary annex reports otherwise: Digit Span Backward at Day 180 is significant on the omnibus test in both the ITT (p=0.02649) and per-protocol (p=0.04779) populations, and the CRB+rTMS vs placebo contrast survives the paper's own Bonferroni adjustment in both (0.0227 and 0.0423). Trail Making Test 1 at Day 180 is also significant on the ITT omnibus (p=0.04012). Two framings both deserve weight and the editorial stage should carry both: (a) the narrative claim is inaccurate as printed; (b) 2-3 results below 0.05 out of 22 uncorrected outcome tests is close to what chance alone predicts, so the underlying inference of 'no effect' may well be right even though the sentence describing it is wrong. Note the direction is conservative -- the paper understates its own positive findings rather than overstating them.

consequence.explanation: The Discussion's claim that no subscale showed a statistically significant difference is contradicted by the paper's own supplementary annex, where Digit Span Backward at Day 180 is significant both before and after Bonferroni adjustment in ITT and PP.

findings.quote: three subscales of the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB): One Touch Stockings of Cambridge, The Multitasking Test, and Reaction Time

computed.note: the corresponding z_ columns exist and feed the composite score

findings.notes: The Methods name 10 co-primary cognitive instruments. Supplementary Annex 1, offered as the complete individual-outcome reporting ('More information is available in the Supplementary Annex 1'), reports group differences for only 11 outcome families covering 7 of those instruments. The three CANTAB subscales -- One Touch Stockings, Multitasking Test and Reaction Time -- have no group-difference analysis anywhere in the paper or the annex, even though their columns are present in the deposited ITT dataset at all three visits AND their z-scores contribute to the composite primary endpoint. So these measures influenced the headline result while never being reported individually. This is a selective-reporting gap, not an arithmetic error.

consequence.explanation: Three of ten stated co-primary instruments contribute to the composite endpoint but have no reported individual analysis, so the claim that individual scales resemble the composite cannot be verified for them.

findings.quote: Replication data for this analysis is published in the Harvard Dataverse, accessible at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/DOFCIV.

reported.dataset: ITT_analysis set, one row per ITT patient, ~120 columns

findings.notes: DELIBERATE DOWNGRADE from the tool's `highly_suspicious` to `indeterminate`; the divergence is recorded rather than silent. Three reasons. (1) The `exclude_columns` argument did not take effect: I passed it twice, as a JSON array and as a comma-separated string, and both runs returned n_columns_excluded=0, excluded_columns=[] and byte-identical output (467,991 characters). So the verdict was computed with SUBJECT ID, GROUP code, SEX and all six date columns INCLUDED -- columns that repeat across patients by design (rulebook rule 11a). (2) The flagged share is a saturation signature, not a duplication signature: 2,260 pairs out of the 3,655 possible pairs among 86 patients is roughly 62% of the entire pair space. A genuine copy-paste artifact is rare and localised; a detector firing on the majority of all pairs is describing the data type. (3) The sheet is a wide table of bounded low-cardinality cognitive scores (MoCA, digit span forward/backward, Hamilton depression and anxiety totals) alongside z-score transforms of those very columns, so every raw-score collision is counted again in its derived column (rule 11b, 11c). Notably the tool found ZERO repeated column sequences and ZERO repeated high-precision values -- the two signals that would indicate real copy-paste. No duplication finding is asserted against this paper.

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected; this records that the raw-data duplication check could not be run under correct exclusions and returns no evidence against the paper.

findings.location: Materials and methods, power paragraph
findings.quote: The total required sample size for the study was determined to be 30 patients per group, including a 10% enhancement for potential dropouts. This sample size allows for the detection of a medium-sized difference between groups with an 80% power.

computed.two_sample_t_note: tool reports the one-tailed requirement does not reconcile either

findings.notes: Recomputed under the two standard readings of 'a medium-sized difference between groups': a three-group one-way ANOVA at Cohen's f=0.25 requires 53 per group (achieved power 0.54 at n=30), and a two-group comparison at d=0.5 requires 64 per group (achieved power 0.48). Neither reconciles with 30 per group, and the tool explicitly checked and rejected the one-tailed reading for the t-test case. STATED CAVEAT, which the editorial stage must carry: the paper did not use either procedure. It used Nnpar 1.0, a non-parametric MULTIVARIATE sample-size method that pools information across 10 correlated outcome scales at rho=0.4, and such a method can legitimately require fewer subjects than a univariate test. So this is a finding that the published power statement cannot be reproduced from the parameters given, not a demonstration that it is arithmetically wrong. Mitigating context: the paper repeatedly concedes the point itself -- 'Given the low sample size of the trial that would inherently lead to the low power of reported analyses' -- so the underpowering is disclosed rather than hidden.

consequence.explanation: The claim that 30 per group affords 80% power to detect a medium effect cannot be reproduced under any standard univariate reading of the stated parameters.

findings.location: Results, adverse events paragraph and Table 1, SAE columns
findings.quote: One serious adverse event (SAE) was reported for the CRB + SHM group.

computed.interpretation: a Kruskal-Wallis omnibus plus three Dunn post-hoc contrasts computed on a variable taking value 1 for exactly one patient and 0 for the other 85

inputs.table: Table 1, SAE Z / P.unadj / P.adj columns

findings.notes: A design/analysis observation, not an arithmetic error -- the numbers are internally consistent (the Dunn Z of exactly 0.000000 with p=1.0 for CRB+rTMS vs PLC+SHM correctly reflects both arms having zero SAEs). The point is that a rank-based omnibus test and three post-hoc contrasts on a variable with a single non-zero observation among 86 patients cannot detect any difference whatever, so the reported p=0.355 carries no evidential content about comparative safety. This matters because tolerability is a headline conclusion of the paper ('safe and well-tolerated'), and it rests on tests that were incapable of returning any other answer. Compounding this, the paper reports no confidence intervals anywhere, so the largest harm difference still compatible with the data cannot be bounded (see the absence_of_evidence entry in `unchecked`).

consequence.explanation: The abstract and Discussion conclusion that the combined intervention is safe and well tolerated rests partly on a significance test that a single event renders uninformative.

findings.quote: Homogeneity analyses for baseline were performed based on the ITT population. In case of heterogeneities, stratified analyses were performed as second-line analyses.

baseline_data_reported: mean age per arm in prose (55.46, 51.04, 49.87)
reported.acknowledged_imbalance: the Cerebrolysin and sham group was roughly five years older, on average

findings.notes: The trial states it is reported per the CONSORT 2010 extension for multi-arm trials, but there is no baseline characteristics table (CONSORT item 15). Only mean ages in prose and a gender figure are given -- no SDs, no per-arm ns, no baseline comparisons. Two consequences. First, the two Table-1-integrity checks this toolkit exists to run, csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion, have no input and cannot be run at all; the usual baseline-similarity forensics are therefore unavailable for this trial, which is a hole in this review rather than a clean result. Second, the paper pre-specifies stratified second-line analyses 'in case of heterogeneities' and then acknowledges a heterogeneity -- an age imbalance of roughly five years -- in the Discussion, yet no stratified or age-adjusted analysis is reported anywhere. That is an unexplained departure from the stated analysis plan.

consequence.explanation: The pre-specified stratified analysis triggered by the acknowledged age imbalance is not reported, so the primary comparison is never adjusted for the one baseline difference the authors themselves flag.

findings.quote: The study enrolled 93 individuals who had suffered traumatic brain injury 30 days before screening.

reported.per_arm_ns_given: only for the composite complete-case subset: PLC + SHM 24, CRB + SHM 20, CRB + rTMS 20

inputs.searched: Results, Methods, Tables 1-2, Supplementary Annex 1, figure captions

findings.notes: A three-arm parallel-group RCT reported under CONSORT never states how many patients were randomised to each arm, nor the per-arm ITT or per-protocol sizes (CONSORT items 13a and 16). The only per-arm ns anywhere are 24/20/20 for the 64-patient complete-case subset used in the composite analysis. This has a direct forensic cost: without per-arm denominators, most percentage- and proportion-based checks (GRIM on any per-arm rate, reconstruct_2x2 on the adverse-event distribution) cannot be run at all, and a reader cannot judge whether allocation was balanced. It also means the 22 ITT patients dropped from the composite analysis (26% of the ITT set) cannot be located by arm.

consequence.explanation: Absent per-arm denominators, neither allocation balance nor differential attrition across the three arms can be assessed by any reader or tool.

Two of the 22 ITT omnibus tests fall below 0.05, which is close to the 1.1 expected by chance -- so the multiplicity burden here most likely argues AGAINST reading the significant Digit Span Backward result as real, and the editorial stage should weigh it that way rather than as an additional problem. tables_checked: Table 1 (Dunn's test, AEs and SAEs) - XML, 18 body cells, typed at 100% coverage
Table 2 (Dunn's test, composite cognitive outcome z-scores) - XML, 18 body cells, typed at 100% coverage
Supplementary Annex 1 (Data Sheet 1, 3 pages) - 44 Kruskal-Wallis omnibus results and 132 Dunn Bonferroni-adjusted p-values, read from the SI PDF
Linked replication dataset (Harvard Dataverse DOFCIV), sheet 'ITT_analysis set' - participant-level, ~120 columns, 7,738 numeric cells, swept via detect_raw_duplication

unchecked.location: Table 1 and Table 2, Dunn's test Z statistics (12 values) vs their unadjusted p-values
unchecked.reason: No validated tool in this kit converts a standard-normal Z to a two-sided p-value. check_regression could be coerced by passing Z as b and 1 as SE, but that is an improvised substitute rather than a fitted check, so it was not run. The Bonferroni relation between P.unadj and P.adj WAS verified for all six non-capped cells.

unchecked.location: Results, composite outcome paragraph: Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared 5.732 and 5.833; Supplementary Annex 1, all 44 chi-squared/df/p triples
unchecked.reason: No tool converts a chi-squared statistic plus df to a p-value. recalc_chi_squared requires a contingency table (unavailable -- these are rank statistics) and recalc_f_to_p would require me to divide the chi-squared by its df, which is computing an F myself. The Day 180 discrepancy was therefore adjudicated by bracketing against the paper's OWN printed chi-squared/p pairs at df=2, and is recorded as a reading rather than a recomputation.

The paper contains no baseline characteristics table and reports no baseline comparison p-values, so the baseline-similarity forensics have no input at all. This is the single largest blind spot in this review: the Carlisle/Fujii-style checks that would normally be the strongest evidence about a randomized trial could not be run.

unchecked.location: All efficacy outcomes (check_effect_plausibility, absence_of_evidence, check_estimate_ci, check_sd_range, check_sd_or_se)
unchecked.reason: The paper reports no group means, no standard deviations and no confidence intervals for any outcome -- results are given only as Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared values, Dunn Z statistics and p-values. No effect size can be computed and the 'no significant difference' and 'safe and well tolerated' conclusions cannot be bounded, because absence_of_evidence requires an interval and none exists. The only interval estimates in the paper are the notched 95% CIs drawn in Figures 3 and 4, which are not printed numerically anywhere.

GRIM deliberately NOT applied. Age here is continuous, not integer: the deposited dataset derives AGE from BRTHDT and PRESDT date columns. GRIM applies only to integer-valued observations, and running it on a continuous measure is the most common route to a false accusation. Independently, the per-arm ns needed for GRIM are never reported.

unchecked.location: All p-values in Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Annex 1 (GRIM-U rank-sum granularity)
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not applied. GRIM-U is valid only for Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum p-values with stated group sizes n1 and n2. These are Kruskal-Wallis omnibus and Dunn post-hoc p-values, which use the pooled rank variance across all three groups, so the granularity argument does not hold. Applying it here would be the top false-accusation risk for this paper.

unchecked.location: Multiplicity correction across the 22 outcome-by-timepoint families (multiplicity_report)
unchecked.reason: TOOL DEFECT, not a property of the paper. multiplicity_report returned n_tests=0 for both the 22-test ITT family and the 22-test PP family; a minimal probe of three bare {p_value} objects also returned 0, confirming the tests payload is not being deserialized. Family-wise error rate, Bonferroni/Holm/BH/BY thresholds and the surviving-claims interval could not be computed, and I did not substitute hand arithmetic.

unchecked.location: Linked replication dataset, duplication analysis under correct column exclusions (detect_raw_duplication)
unchecked.reason: TOOL DEFECT. exclude_columns had no effect when passed as a JSON array or as a comma-separated string -- both runs reported n_columns_excluded=0 and excluded_columns=[] and produced byte-identical 467,991-character output. The verdict could only be obtained with SUBJECT, GROUP, SEX and six date columns included, which repeat across patients by design, so no trustworthy duplication verdict is available for this dataset.

The annex prints only ADJUSTED p-values, not the unadjusted ones, so the P.adj = 3 x P.unadj relation verified for the main tables cannot be checked here. The adjusted values were read and used for interpretation but the adjustment arithmetic is unverifiable as printed.

Figure extraction was not run; values were not read off the plots. All four figures carry numbers that appear nowhere in the text or tables -- per-arm sex counts (Fig 1), age medians and quartiles (Fig 2), and the composite primary endpoint's distribution and notched 95% confidence intervals at both timepoints (Figs 3, 4). The primary endpoint's interval estimates therefore went unchecked in this review.

unchecked.location: Secondary outcomes: eye tracking (Tobii Pro TX300) and EEG
unchecked.reason: Collected but explicitly deferred: 'Since these secondary measures require distinct data processing and specialized analysis, they will be reported in subsequent manuscripts.' No statistics are given, so nothing is checkable. Noted because measures collected but never analysed are a reporting pattern worth an editor's attention.

unchecked.location: Per-arm randomized, ITT and per-protocol sample sizes
unchecked.reason: Never reported by the paper for any of the three arms, so percentage-based checks (grim_percentage on per-arm rates, reconstruct_2x2 on the adverse-event distribution across arms) had no denominator and could not be run.
